story.headline: Gulf attacks spread on Thanksgiving, as drones killed two Italian workers in Kuwait and a Houthi strike halted part of a Saudi refinery. Oil held near $95 while currencies barely moved in thin holiday trade.

reads.policy: A December Fed hike stays all but certain, and the European Central Bank's October notes confirm a December rise there too. Euro-area leaders picked a centrist to lead the European Central Bank from February, and every big Canadian bank now expects a Bank of Canada hike.
reads.growth: Australian firms stepped up investment far more than expected, and the Fed's Beige Book found most US regions still growing. German consumers stayed deeply gloomy. Strong growth backs higher rates in the US and Australia, while Europe lags.
reads.inflation: US core inflation edged up again in October, and Australian inflation is climbing. In Japan, a rate-setter said a weak yen and costly raw materials are pushing prices up, ahead of Tokyo's November figures tonight. All three keep their central banks leaning against easing.
reads.risk: The Gulf fighting spread, with deadly attacks in Kuwait and on a Saudi refinery, but markets looked past it in thin holiday trade. European shares rose and the franc lost ground against the euro. The Bank of England warned that borrowing to fund artificial intelligence is a growing risk to the financial system.
reads.tot: Oil held near $95 as attacks around the Gulf kept supply fears alive, though no barrels were lost. That helps the Canadian dollar and costs Japan and the euro area. Gold steadied after bouncing from its lowest in more than a year.
reads.positioning: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds have turned slightly against the dollar, while still betting against the euro, the kiwi, the franc and, most strongly, the Canadian dollar. They still bet on the pound and the Aussie, where big long-term investors take the opposite side. Heavy bets against the loonie leave room for a fast unwind if Canadian hike bets keep growing.
reads.fiscal: The US plans new tariffs on 14 economies, but nothing takes effect before early 2027. France's debts remain a weight on the euro, with S&P due to review its credit rating on Friday, November 27.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike, and most officials now expect more hikes. Traders fully expect a quarter-point hike on December 9, with another in January a little more likely than not.
fed.priced: December: quarter-point hike all but certain. January: another hike a little more likely than not.
fed.why: US growth was revised up to a 4.3% pace and core inflation rose to 3.3%, well above the Fed's 2% goal. Falling US bond yields this week show some doubt about how far hikes go after December.
fed.watch: October's US trade figures on Friday, November 27, in a short session after Thanksgiving. The decision is December 9, with new forecasts from officials.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October. Governor Tiff Macklem said on Tuesday, November 24 the bank may need to act sooner, and all six of Canada's biggest banks now expect a December hike.
boc.why: Macklem warned the oil shock will keep prices sticky and said the bank was too slow to spot lasting inflation after the pandemic. Oil holding near $95 a barrel adds to that worry.
boc.watch: Canada's third-quarter growth on Monday, November 30, the jobs report on Friday, December 4, and oil prices. The decision is December 9.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a narrow vote. Rising unemployment has made a December hike less certain, but a jump in shop sales in the third quarter strengthens the case for one.
rbnz.priced: December: hike possible but not fully expected.
rbnz.why: Inflation pressures and stronger spending argue for a hike, while unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for waiting. Governor Anna Breman gave no clear signal on December in her latest speech.
rbnz.watch: The official election result on Friday, November 27 and the next dairy price auction. The decision is December 9.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% in October, and the record of that meeting showed many officials were ready to hike then. A December hike is widely expected, and euro-area leaders picked Pablo Hernández de Cos to succeed President Christine Lagarde in February 2027.
ecb.priced: December: hike widely expected, possibly the last for a while.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal and core prices are firming. Slow German growth, weak factories and France's debts limit how far it can go, and the incoming president is seen as a centrist.
ecb.watch: Spain's and France's November inflation and S&P's review of France's credit rating, all on Friday, November 27. The decision is December 17.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan holds at 1.25%, far below other major banks, and is expected to hike in December. Board member Naoki Tamura said on Thursday, November 26 the bank may need to hike faster if inflation runs hot.
boj.why: Costly raw materials, a weak yen and strong demand are pushing prices up, Tamura said. He is among the keenest on higher rates, so his words mostly confirm what markets expected.
boj.watch: Tokyo's November inflation on Thursday, November 26 at 5:30 PM CT, and any sign Japan steps in near 160 yen. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest among the major banks. Inflation jumped to 4.9% in October and business investment surged, which ended bets on a cut soon.
rba.priced: December: hold expected. Cuts in 2027 now look less likely.
rba.why: Inflation is well above the bank's 2–3% target and firms are still spending hard. Job losses argue for patience, so the bank is expected to hold, with the risk leaning toward another hike rather than a cut.
rba.watch: Australia's third-quarter growth on Wednesday, December 2 (Australian time). The decision is December 8.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5, and markets lean toward another hike on December 17. Its Financial Stability Report on Thursday, November 26 gave no new signal on rates.
boe.why: Governor Andrew Bailey said inflation may peak lower if energy prices hold, while policymaker Catherine Mann wants more hikes sooner. High fuel costs still keep UK inflation near twice the bank's goal.
boe.watch: Any comments from officials, after Governor Andrew Bailey and two colleagues sounded split before lawmakers on Wednesday, November 25. The decision is December 17.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and can sell francs if they get too strong. Low Swiss inflation means no hike is in sight.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is low, so the bank has no reason to raise rates and some room to cut if the franc climbs.
snb.watch: Falls in stock markets or Gulf flare-ups that send money into the franc, and the new US tariff plans for Swiss goods. The decision is December 10.

AUD.summary: The Aussie sits at the top of the board, thanks to the highest interest rates among the major central banks. Hot inflation and a surge in business investment make cuts unlikely, though nervous markets kept it near its lowest this year.

GBP.summary: The pound sits second on the board because UK interest rates are among the highest of the eight, and markets lean toward another Bank of England hike in December. It still trades near a one-year low against the dollar.

USD.summary: The dollar sits third on the board. High US interest rates and a fast-growing economy support it, while large budget deficits weigh. Falling US bond yields this week trimmed its edge, though a December Fed hike is still fully expected.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits fourth, in the middle of the board. Firm dairy prices help, but doubts over a December rate hike and nervous markets keep it near a 17-year low against the US dollar.

EUR.summary: The euro sits fifth, just below the middle of the board. Germany's economy is barely growing and France's debts hold the euro back. It trades near $1.10, not far above its weakest in about 19 months.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits sixth, in the lower half of the board, because recent Canadian data has mostly missed forecasts. Firmer oil and a widely expected December Bank of Canada hike have lifted it to near a two-week high against the US dollar.

JPY.summary: The yen sits second from the bottom because Japanese interest rates are far below the others. A likely December Bank of Japan hike and the threat of Japan stepping in keep the dollar just under 160 yen.

CHF.summary: The franc sits at the bottom of the board. Swiss interest rates are the lowest of the eight and inflation is too low to need higher rates. It gains when fear sends money its way, and gives that back when markets calm.
